description:
We are an ambitious project team participating in NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026, combining expertise in software engineering, AI/data solutions, and core application development.

Our goal is to build an impactful, scalable, and technology-driven open-source solution to address real-world space and Earth challenges. We welcome passionate collaborators across engineering, data, design, and domain research who are driven to solve complex problems and ship a great demo.
summary: Echoes of Silence is an interactive, browser-based 1:1 metric-scale 3D museum and WebRTC AR exhibition that transforms 13 inactive NASA spacecraft across the Moon, Mars, Asteroid 433 Eros, Dwarf Planet Ceres, and Deep Space into living, first-person STEM storytellers. Over six decades of exploration have left historic landers, rovers, and probes resting silently on distant worlds, where raw coordinate tables often make them feel like forgotten "space junk" to young learners. Our web application bridges this gap through three connected perspectives: a 3D Solar System Explorer showing real transfer trajectories and speed-of-light radio delays, an Orbital Museum Deck comparing all 13 spacecraft side-by-side, and a 1:1 Planetary Surface Stage where students stand beside each machine next to a 1.75m astronaut, compare historic mission photos with modern orbital reconnaissance, and interview the spacecraft in the first person.
details:
1. WHAT DOES IT DO & HOW DOES IT WORK?

Echoes of Silence is a zero-install, browser-based 3D and Web AR exhibition that turns 13 silent NASA spacecraft across 5 celestial destinations (the Moon, Mars, Asteroid 433 Eros, Dwarf Planet 1 Ceres, and Deep Space) into interactive, first-person teachers. Users explore through three seamless spatial modes:

• Mode 1 — 3D Solar System Explorer: An interactive heliocentric map where an animated JPL-style transfer spacecraft flies along mission transfer arcs (Translunar Injection, Hohmann Mars Transfer, and Deep-Space Ion Spirals) while displaying real-time one-way speed-of-light radio communication delays from Earth (from 1.28 Light-Seconds at the Moon to ~18.6 Light-Hours in Deep Space).

• Mode 2 — Orbital Museum Deck: A curated exhibition gallery placing all 13 spacecraft side-by-side on illuminated pedestals with category filters (Landers, Rovers, Probes, and Instruments) so learners can compare 57 years of aerospace engineering.

• Mode 3 — 1:1 Surface Stage & Live Mobile AR: Places users on reconstructed Lunar regolith, Martian iron-oxide dust, or asteroid terrain at true metric scale (1 unit = 1 meter) beside a 1.75m astronaut scale reference or in live mobile WebRTC camera passthrough. Clicking any spacecraft opens 39 interactive 3D engineering pins, a "Then vs. Now" switcher comparing historic surface photos with overhead LROC and MRO HiRISE satellite reconnaissance, and "Ask the Spacecraft" interactive Q&A chips.

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE & WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

• Multi-Tier Educational Impact: Designed across three learning tiers—Young Explorers (Ages 10–14) engage with empathetic first-person stories ("I landed...", "My solar panels...") and earn a printable 13/13 Explorer Passport Certificate; High School STEM students analyze orbital mechanics, light-time delays, and environmental failure modes; and Educators gain a free, 15-minute browser lab with zero installation or login walls.

• Space Heritage Preservation: Reframes inactive planetary hardware from "discarded equipment" into protected scientific monuments and time capsules of human ingenuity.

3. TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES & SOFTWARE USED

• Frontend & 3D Engine: React 19, TypeScript, Three.js (r183), React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber), @react-three/drei, and custom GLSL atmospheric Fresnel and solar corona shaders.

• Styling, UI & AR: Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide React icons, HTML5 Canvas procedural planetary surface maps, Web Speech API, and WebRTC navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia for live mobile AR camera passthrough.

• Build & Deployment: Vite 8, Git/GitHub, and Vercel.

• Live App Link: https://spaghetti-coders.vercel.app

• GitHub Repository: https://github.com/omarsh4114/NASA-Abandoned-Not-Forgotten-404

4. HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE & WHAT FACTORS DID OUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Instead of presenting static encyclopedia pages, we gave each spacecraft its own first-person voice so students can "interview" the hardware about what it discovered and why it went silent. We also engineered a true 1:1 metric scale comparison beside a 1.75m human astronaut so learners immediately grasp that Mars's Sojourner rover (0.65m) is the size of a microwave oven while Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage (4.20m wide) towers like a two-story cabin. To ensure 100% classroom reliability even on restricted school networks, we built an automatic SVG NASA Telemetry Blueprint fallback plate.

5. TRANSPARENT AI / SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

Team Spaghetti Coders (Omar, Bashar, and Youssef) conceived the project architecture and curatorial design independently. Google Antigravity and Google Gemini assisted with Three.js/React code scaffolding, custom GLSL shader tuning, and copyediting historical mission summaries into age-appropriate first-person educational narratives. Manus AI assisted with structuring our 7-slide presentation deck. Zero AI-generated images or altered NASA logos are used anywhere; all telemetry and archival imagery originate from official public-domain NASA datasets.
